title: No Work, No Food
text:
Hyakujo, the Chinese Zen master known in China as Baizhang, kept working alongside his pupils even when he was eighty years old. Every day he went out with them to trim the gardens, clean the grounds and prune the trees.

The pupils felt sorry to see the old teacher working so hard. They knew he would not listen if they told him to stop, so they hid his tools.

That day the master did not eat. The next day he did not eat, nor the day after. The pupils began to worry. Perhaps he was angry that they had hidden his tools. They decided they had better put them back.

The day they returned the tools, the master worked and ate the same as before. In the evening he explained to them: "No work, no food."
lesson: Asking others to work while exempting yourself teaches them that work is for lesser people. Doing your share, even when you could skip it, makes your standards believable.
source: 101 Zen Stories, compiled by Nyogen Senzaki and Paul Reps (1919)
caveat: The saying "a day without work is a day without food" is traditionally attributed to Baizhang, but the anecdote comes from later Zen literature.
